tagline: From Idaho’s highest summit country to lava fields beside an emigrant trail
intro: Peaks to Craters is a two-lane drive with some passing lanes, linking the Lost River Mountains with farmland and lava fields. Visit Idaho features it among the state’s scenic byways and highlights Mount Borah, Craters of the Moon and Arco’s atomic-energy history. Its 2024 guide lists 143 miles and two hours, 27 minutes.

An older journey survives beside the highway near the lava fields. In 1852, John Jeffrey promoted a trail following traditional Shoshoni paths to bring business to his Blackfoot River ferry. Tim Goodale led 1,095 people and 338 wagons over the cutoff in 1862. Goodale’s Cutoff remains visible at points beside US 20, 26 and 93 between Craters of the Moon and Carey.
At Craters of the Moon, road development followed the creation of the national monument in 1924. The Mission 66 program began construction of the park’s road system and visitor center in 1956.

For a north-to-south drive, begin at US 93’s junction with Idaho 75 south of Challis and wind through Grandview Canyon toward Borah Peak. Continue through Mackay to Arco on the Big Lost River. The combined highways cross the monument’s northwestern part, then reach Carey on the Little Wood River before the Idaho 75 junction.

moments.title: Borah Peak
moments.text: Borah Peak, Idaho’s highest summit, stands 12,662 feet high in the central Lost River Range, within Challis National Forest in eastern Custer County. The U.S. Geological Survey named it for Senator William Borah in February 1934, after it was found to exceed Hyndman Peak, previously considered the state’s highest point. The landscape changed again on October 28, 1983, when an earthquake raised the peak about a foot and lowered the nearby valley about eight feet. A scar remains visible on its western side. In Challis, falling masonry killed two children walking to school.

moments.title: Arco
moments.text: Number Hill carries a record of Arco’s graduating classes in paint. Since 1920, each Butte County High School class has painted its graduation year on the rocky slope. A different milestone came on July 17, 1955, when Arco became the first community in the world lit solely by nuclear-generated electricity. That demonstration lasted about an hour, supplied by Argonne National Laboratory’s BORAX-III reactor at the nearby National Reactor Testing Station. The station is now Idaho National Laboratory, part of the town’s economic base alongside agriculture and recreation. Arco sits along the Big Lost River, between the Snake River Plain and the Lost River Range.
moments.notice: The painted graduation years cover Number Hill’s rocky face.

moments.title: Craters of the Moon
moments.text: Sixty solidified lava flows make up the Craters of the Moon Lava Field. They erupted along the Great Rift, a zone of weakness in the Earth’s crust. The forms record different movements of molten rock: pasty blobs built spatter cones, while streams left lava tubes after their crusts hardened and the liquid drained away. Elsewhere, lava overran trees; water released as they burned cooled the rock enough to preserve impressions. Some molds retain shapes of bark, a record of the forest consumed by the flow. The through highway cuts across the monument’s northwestern part; within the rugged landscape, the single paved road crosses its northern end.

practical: Craters of the Moon: Snow drifts close the park’s Loop Road to vehicle traffic in winter. (checked 2026-10-11)
